h1: Do you need a science background to become a brewer?
title: Do you need a science degree to brew? | Craft Beer School
desc: You do not have to be a scientist to start brewing. Learn which science helps, when it matters and where a first-time learner should begin.
teaser: No degree needed to start. Some science helps later. You can learn it as you go.
standfirst: Brewing looks like chemistry and biology. Parts of it are. That does not mean you must have studied either to begin. This guide explains where science matters and how a beginner can start without it.
sections:
You can start learning to brew without a science background. Many of the ideas are simple once someone explains them plainly: grain gives sugar, yeast turns sugar into alcohol and hops add bitterness and aroma. What a science background does give you is speed on the harder topics later on.

Whether a particular job needs a degree is a different question. Employers differ, so read our guide on brewing careers for microbiology and food technology graduates as well as this one.

Think of brewing as a craft with a science underneath it. You can drive a car without knowing how the engine works, but a mechanic needs to know. Beginners are in the driver's seat. People who run a brewhouse eventually need to look under the bonnet.
The science you will actually use

Day to day, brewers use a small set of ideas. Temperature affects what the mash makes: 62 to 65 °C gives a drier beer while 68 to 70 °C gives more body. Acidity matters too: mash pH should sit between 5.2 and 5.6. Gravity readings let you work out ABV from your own numbers. Cleaning and sanitising keep unwanted microbes out of the beer.

Most of this is arithmetic and careful habit. You do not need a degree to learn it. You need a teacher who explains each step and lets you practise.

Later topics lean on chemistry and microbiology. Reading a water lab report, controlling esters, fusels and diacetyl in fermentation and writing a QA plan all use deeper science. That is the territory of Advanced Brewing Science, our six-week online course (₹12,999). It is written for working brewers, graduates of Brewing Fundamentals and serious homebrewers.

A science graduate may move through the early material faster. A career switcher from sales, finance or hospitality may need more time on it but can get there. Your background changes the pace, not whether you can learn.

Brewing Fundamentals is built for this. It runs four weeks online (8 live sessions of 2 hours) for ₹5,999. Week by week it covers grain to glass, malt, water and the mash, hops, boil and yeast and then sanitation, kit and your first recipe. It is written for homebrewers, beer lovers ready to brew a first real recipe or hospitality and sales people who talk about beer. For exact entry requirements, ask us.

If you want a gentler first look, Beer for Starters is a one-hour online course at ₹199.

The live format helps too. Sessions run on Saturdays and Sundays, 12:00 PM to 2:00 PM IST, with a maximum of 20 students. You can ask a question the moment something confuses you. The recordings let you revisit a topic.

Plenty of people come to brewing from other fields in their thirties or forties. Read our guide for career switchers for the practical side. For a map of every course against your background, our course chooser is the place to look.

"I must know chemistry first." You do not. The chemistry you meet in a first course is explained as it comes up. It is mostly cause and effect: change the mash temperature and the beer changes.

"Brewers are all scientists." Some are. Many are people who learned the craft by doing it, then added the science when a problem demanded it. A hard-to-explain stuck mash or a stubborn off-flavour pushes most brewers to learn more.

"Without a degree, nobody will take me seriously." We cannot speak for every employer. We cannot promise any job. What we can say is that clear understanding, careful records and clean habits are what a brewhouse notices first.

A low-cost way to test your comfort is to do the free Safety in Brewing course first, then Beer for Starters, then decide on Brewing Fundamentals.
Tell us what you studied, what you do now and what you want brewing to become. We will suggest whether Brewing Fundamentals is the right starting point or whether something smaller makes more sense.
faqs: Can I become a brewer without a degree?
You can learn to brew without one. Whether a specific employer asks for a degree varies, so check before you apply.
Is Brewing Fundamentals hard for non-science students?
It is written to explain each step plainly, so people from other fields can follow it. If you are worried about a topic, ask us.
Basic arithmetic is enough to start. You will calculate things like ABV from gravity readings. The course shows you how.
